hints: Think about what the word monodentate means, mono means one, so how many points of attachment can this ligand make to the metal?
Recall what any ligand must have to bond to a metal ion, and what name is given to the bond where both shared electrons come from the ligand.
walkthrough:
Picture what a ligand does**
Imagine the metal ion like $\text{Ag}^{+}$ sitting in the middle with empty orbitals waiting for electrons. A ligand is a particle that has a lone pair it can share. It pushes that lone pair into the empty orbital on the metal.

Add the meaning of mono**
Mono means one, so a monodentate ligand uses only one lone pair to make only one bond to the metal. Because both electrons in that shared bond come from the ligand, you call it a dative or coordinate bond to the central metal atom or ion.
Final answer: A species that donates one lone pair to form a dative / coordinate bond to a central metal atom / metal ion.

hints: A linear complex has coordination number 2, so link how many $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ ligands must surround one $\text{Ag}^{+}$ ion and then add up the charges.
walkthrough:
Work out the coordination number from the shape**
Linear always means two ligands arranged at $180^{\circ}$, one on each side of the metal. So $\text{P}$ must contain one $\text{Ag}^{+}$ joined to two $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ ligands.

Balance the charges**
Add them up: $(+1) + 2 \times (-2) = -3$. Put the metal and ligands inside square brackets to show it is a complex ion: $[\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$.

hints: Identify the reactant complex $\text{P}$ and the incoming $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligand, and remember $\text{Q}$ is the analogous linear cyano complex $[\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^{-}$ with $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ released.
walkthrough:
Spot the swap**
You start with $[\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$ and you add $\text{CN}^{-}$. The cyanide ions take the place of the thiosulfate ions around the same $\text{Ag}^{+}$. Because the product $\text{Q}$ is also linear, it needs two $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands: $[\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^{-}$.

Write it balanced**
Two $\text{CN}^{-}$ go in, so two $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ must come out: $$[\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-} + 2\text{CN}^{-} \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^{-} + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$$ Check atoms and charge: $-5$ on each side, so it balances.

hints: If almost all of $\text{P}$ is converted into $\text{Q}$, think about which complex holds onto the $\text{Ag}^{+}$ ion more strongly and what that says about its stability constant.
walkthrough:
Read the position of equilibrium**
You are told $[\text{Q}]$ is much greater than $[\text{P}]$ after mixing. That means the equilibrium for $\text{P}$ changing to $\text{Q}$ lies far to the right.

Link to stability**
A complex that forms in preference to another is the more thermodynamically stable one. So $[\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]^{-}$ must bind $\text{Ag}^{+}$ more strongly than $[\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$, which means $\text{Q}$ has the larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ value.
Final answer: $\text{Q}$ is more stable / has a larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ than $\text{P}$.

hints: Focus on what happens to the ligands, one type leaves the metal and a different type takes its place, what general name is given to that swap?
walkthrough:
Name the swap**
The $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ ligands are pushed out and $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands go in, but the metal $\text{Ag}^{+}$ and the coordination number stay the same. Whenever one ligand directly replaces another like this, you call it ligand exchange, also accepted as ligand displacement or ligand substitution.
Final answer: Ligand exchange / displacement / substitution.

hints: With formula $[\text{Pt}(\text{CN})_2Cl_2]^{2-}$ and four ligands around Pt, sketch a square with Pt in the centre and place the two $\text{CN}$ groups next to each other for one isomer and opposite each other for the other.
walkthrough:
Set up the square**
Put $\text{Pt}$ in the centre of a square with four corners for ligands. You have two identical $\text{CN}$ ligands (bond through C) and two identical $Cl$ ligands.

Draw the two different arrangements**
In the cis isomer, put the two $\text{CN}$ groups on adjacent corners, for example top left and bottom left, with the two $Cl$ groups on the other two adjacent corners. In the trans isomer, put the two $\text{CN}$ groups opposite each other, for example top left and bottom right, with the two $Cl$ groups opposite each other on the remaining corners.

Final answer: One isomer with the two $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands adjacent (cis, $90^{\circ}$ apart) and the two $Cl^{-}$ ligands adjacent; one isomer with the two $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands opposite (trans, $180^{\circ}$ apart) and the two $Cl^{-}$ ligands opposite. Pt at centre, C of $\text{CN}$ bonded to Pt.

hints: A four coordinate complex that shows cis-trans isomerism with only two isomers cannot be tetrahedral, so what flat 90 degree geometry must Pt(II) adopt?
walkthrough:
Use the isomer evidence**
A tetrahedral $[\text{Pt}(\text{CN})_2Cl_2]^{2-}$ would have all positions equivalent and would show only one form. The fact you can isolate cis and trans forms proves the four bonds point to the corners of a square in one plane with bond angles of $90^{\circ}$, which is square planar, typical for $\text{Pt(II)}$.

hints: Recall the name for stereoisomerism in square planar complexes where the difference is whether identical ligands are side by side or across from each other.
walkthrough:
Name the pattern**
The two structures have the same bonds but different spatial arrangements of the $\text{CN}^{-}$ and $Cl^{-}$ groups around the $\text{Pt}$. When identical ligands can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans) in a square planar complex, it is called cis-trans isomerism, also called geometrical isomerism.
